# Scaling up {#sec-scaling}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

The example in @sec-manuscript is a real pipeline in miniature: eighteen simulations,
a figure, a table, two documents. A real methods paper is the same shape with the
numbers changed --- a few hundred simulation jobs, seventeen figures and tables,
results measured in days of compute rather than seconds. This chapter is about what
changes and what does not.

Almost nothing about the Snakefile changes. What changes is where things live.

## Two repositories

The natural instinct is to put everything in the manuscript's repository. That works
until the second paper, at which point you find yourself copying the estimator into
a new directory and maintaining two versions of it.

The structure that holds up splits the work in two:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart TB
  subgraph M["manuscript repo"]
    S[Snakefile]
    T[main.tex]
    C[code/figure1.R ...]
  end
  subgraph R["methods repo (an R package)"]
    F[R/ -- the estimators]
    Q[scripts/ -- one per simulation]
  end
  S -->|runs| Q
  Q -->|writes| D[(rds/ -- cached results)]
  D --> C
  C --> T
```

**The methods repository is an R package.** `R/` holds the estimators, with the
usual `DESCRIPTION` and `NAMESPACE`, so it can be installed, tested, versioned and
cited on its own. `scripts/` holds one script per kind of simulation, each taking
`optparse` flags and writing one `.rds` named for its parameters --- exactly the
scripts of @sec-rscript, just more of them.

**The manuscript repository holds the paper**: the `.tex` files, the scripts that
draw each figure, and the Snakefile that ties it together. Its rules call the *other*
repository's scripts.

The payoff is that the estimator has one home. The next paper gets a new manuscript
repository and reuses the package; a reader who wants the method installs the
package and ignores the paper entirely.

## Pointing at the other repository

The Snakefile needs to know where the methods repository is, and coauthors keep it
in different places. The straightforward approach is a config value:

```{.yaml filename="config.yaml"}
res-loc: "~/repos/lasso-confint/"
```

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
import os
LOC = os.path.expanduser(config["res-loc"])

rule distribution_results:
    input:
        script = f"{LOC}scripts/distribution_results.R"
    output:
        f"{LOC}rds/{ITER}/original/{{distribution}}_{{n}}_{{method}}.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} --n {wildcards.n} --method {wildcards.method} "
        "--loc {LOC}"
```

Two things to notice. The `f` prefix makes a Python f-string, where `{LOC}` is
substituted immediately; wildcards, which must survive to be matched later, are
written `{{n}}` to escape them. And `--loc {LOC}` passes the location to the R
script too, so that it can find the package and write its results in the right
place.

If your collaborators will not maintain a config file, you can look the path up by
username instead:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
import getpass
LOC = {
    "pbreheny": "~/res/lasso-confint/",
    "hlogan":   "~/repos/lasso-confint/",
}.get(getpass.getuser(), "~/res/lasso-confint/")
```

This is what `man-avg-cov` does, and it is genuinely convenient for a small group.
It also stops working the moment someone new joins, so treat it as a default that
the config can override rather than the only mechanism.

## Results outside the repository

Notice that the `.rds` files in that layout live in the *methods* repository, not
the manuscript's. This is the same idea as the `results/` folder the examples in
this book have been writing to since @sec-rscript, moved one step further out: at
this scale the results are shared by several manuscripts, so they belong with
neither of them in particular.

A simulation that takes two days to run is not a build artifact in the way a figure
is. You do not want it deleted when you clean the manuscript directory, you want it
shared between the paper and the talk and the grant renewal, and you do not want it
in git. Keeping the cache in one place --- keyed by parameters, so a run for
`n = 400` is never confused with a run for `n = 100` --- gets you all three.

The iteration count is part of the path for the same reason:

```
rds/1000/original/laplace_autoregressive_0_100_101_gaussian_100_pipep.rds
    ^^^^
```

so the 20-iteration smoke test and the 1000-iteration final run coexist, and
switching between them is a config edit rather than an act of destruction.

### Sharing the folder

Once every result is under one roof, sharing the project's output is a matter of
sharing one directory. Which raises the question of how.

Email and Dropbox both work and both go wrong in the same way: somebody edits a
file you were about to overwrite, and the loser never finds out. Git is the tool
you would reach for, except that git is bad at exactly this kind of content. A
few hundred megabytes of `.rds` files will bloat the repository permanently, diff
and merge do nothing useful on serialized objects, and results derived from
protected health information have no business on GitHub at all.

[`dat`](https://github.com/pbreheny/dat) is built for this gap. It gives a
directory a git-style push/pull workflow backed by S3, without keeping version
history:

```bash
cd results
dat init
dat push
```

and on a collaborator's machine:

```bash
dat clone jsmith7.snakemake.tutorial results
dat pull
```

The part that makes it more than a wrapper around `rsync` is that it detects
conflicts: if someone has modified a file you are about to overwrite, it says so
rather than silently clobbering their work. It hashes file contents, so pushing a
directory where one of 400 simulations changed transfers one file. And
`dat status` will tell you whether you are in sync without touching the network.

The pairing is natural. Git holds the code, which is small, textual, and wants
history. `dat` holds the results, which are large, binary, and only ever want to
be *current*. Both are one command to push, and a collaborator with both has your
entire project.

## Chained rules

Expensive intermediate steps become their own rules, rather than being folded into
the script that needs them:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule fit_gam:
    input:
        script = f"{LOC}scripts/fit_gam.R",
        rds    = f"{LOC}rds/{ITER}/original/{{distribution}}_{{n}}_{{method}}.rds"
    output:
        f"{LOC}rds/{ITER}/gam/{{distribution}}_{{n}}_{{method}}.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} --n {wildcards.n} --method {wildcards.method} "
        "--loc {LOC}"
```

The smoothing step reads the simulation output and writes its own file, so
re-tuning the smoother does not rerun the simulation. Every stage you can afford to
separate is a stage you will not have to repeat --- and in a project where the
first stage takes a day, that is the difference between iterating on a figure in
minutes and iterating on it overnight.

## Optional expensive pieces

Some comparisons are too slow to run by default. Make them a switch:

```{.yaml filename="config.yaml"}
desparsified: false   # adds hours; needed only for the final version
```

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
DESPARSIFIED = config.get("desparsified", False)

rule figure5:
    input:
        rds = expand(
            f"{LOC}rds/{ITER}/gam/laplace_{{method}}.rds",
            method = ["pipep", "selectiveinferenceS"] +
                     (["desparsified"] if DESPARSIFIED else [])
        )
```

The list of inputs is computed by Python, so a flag in the config changes which jobs
exist at all. The figure script gets the same flag and adjusts its legend
accordingly. Someone reproducing your results gets something in an hour by default,
and everything if they are willing to wait.

## What this buys you

A `README` for a project of this shape can honestly say:

> With Snakemake installed, `snakemake --cores=1` runs the simulations and builds
> the manuscript. Start with `snakemake figure1` to confirm your setup works.

Which is a strong claim, and it is checkable --- by a reviewer, by a reader, and by
you in eighteen months when someone asks where a number came from.

## Where to go next {#sec-next}

Everything in this book runs locally. Three directions to read about when you
outgrow that:

**Clusters.** Snakemake can submit each job to SLURM or SGE instead of running it
locally. This is a *profile* --- a directory containing a `config.yaml` with the
submit command and resource defaults --- plus an executor plugin
(`snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm`, or `-cluster-generic` for SGE). The Snakefile
does not change; you add `--profile slurm` to the command line. Per-rule
`resources: mem_mb=..., runtime=...` become the memory and walltime requests. Note
that this changed substantially in Snakemake 8, so check the version of anything
you read. The [Iowa HPC tutorial](https://iowabiostat.github.io/hpc/12.html) has a
worked SGE example.

**Containers.** A `container:` directive at the top of the Snakefile runs every job
inside a Docker or Apptainer image, which pins your R version and every package
along with it. This is the piece that turns "reproducible on my machine" into
"reproducible".

**Checkpoints.** Everything here assumes the DAG is known before anything runs.
When the set of jobs depends on a result --- fit a model, then run one job per
selected variable --- you need `checkpoint` instead of `rule`, which lets Snakemake
re-plan mid-run.

The [Snakemake documentation](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/) covers all three,
and the [best practices](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/en/stable/snakefiles/best_practices.html)
page is worth a read once the ideas here are comfortable.
